claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is estimated to have evolved within the confines of the human lung for millennia.
source: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the causative pathogen of the pulmonary disease tuberculosis (TB), is estimated to have evolved within the confines of the human lung for millennia (Comas et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Comas et al., 2013

claim: Co-evolution of M. tuberculosis with humans results in a choreographed response of innate and adaptive immune cells culminating in the formation of granulomas.
source: A result of this co-evolution is a choreographed response of innate and adaptive immune cells culminating in the formation of granulomas, specialized structures that permit bacterial replication and ultimately promote transmission (Ramakrishnan, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ramakrishnan, 2012

claim: Granulomas are specialized structures that permit bacterial replication and ultimately promote transmission.
source: A result of this co-evolution is a choreographed response of innate and adaptive immune cells culminating in the formation of granulomas, specialized structures that permit bacterial replication and ultimately promote transmission (Ramakrishnan, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ramakrishnan, 2012

claim: Mycobacteria avoid and manipulate host immune pathways to afford the pathogen safe harbor in otherwise bactericidal myeloid cells.
source: A key strategy used by mycobacteria throughout infection is to avoid and manipulate host immune pathways so as to afford the pathogen safe harbor in otherwise bactericidal myeloid cells (Cambier et al., 2014a; Urdahl, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cambier et al., 2014a and Urdahl, 2014

claim: The zebrafish larva is a natural host of the pathogen M. marinum.
source: To better understand these host–pathogen interactions, we have taken advantage of the optically transparent zebrafish larva, a natural host of the pathogen M. marinum (Ramakrishnan, 2020; Takaki et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ramakrishnan, 2020 and Takaki et al., 2013

claim: Infection of the hindbrain ventricle (HBV) allows for the visualization and characterization of the cellular immune response.
source: Infection of the hindbrain ventricle (HBV), an epithelium-lined cavity, allows for the visualization and characterization of the cellular immune response (Davis and Ramakrishnan, 2009), a response that is comparable to that seen in the mouse lung following infection with M. tuberculosis (Srivastava et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Davis and Ramakrishnan, 2009 and Srivastava et al., 2014

claim: The cellular immune response in zebrafish HBV infection is comparable to that seen in the mouse lung following infection with M. tuberculosis.
source: Infection of the hindbrain ventricle (HBV), an epithelium-lined cavity, allows for the visualization and characterization of the cellular immune response (Davis and Ramakrishnan, 2009), a response that is comparable to that seen in the mouse lung following infection with M. tuberculosis (Srivastava et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Srivastava et al., 2014

claim: In both zebrafish and mouse models, mycobacteria are initially phagocytosed by tissue-resident macrophages and are eventually transferred to monocytes which go on to form granulomas.
source: In both models, mycobacteria are initially phagocytosed by tissue-resident macrophages and are eventually transferred to monocytes which go on to form granulomas (Cambier et al., 2017; Cohen et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cambier et al., 2017 and Cohen et al., 2018

claim: Bactericidal monocytes are recruited downstream of toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling in response to mucosal commensal pathogens.
source: In response to mucosal commensal pathogens, bactericidal monocytes are recruited downstream of toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling (Medzhitov, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Medzhitov, 2007

claim: The cell-surface lipid phthiocerol dimycocerosate (PDIM) is required to evade the antibacterial response.
source: Screening of M. marinum genetic mutants found that the cell-surface lipid phthiocerol dimycocerosate (PDIM) is required to evade this antibacterial response (Cambier et al., 2014b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cambier et al., 2014b

claim: PDIM is required for the relative impermeability of the mycobacterial cell wall.
source: PDIM also promotes pathogenesis in other ways, such as being required for the relative impermeability of the mycobacterial cell wall (Camacho et al., 2001) and in promoting escape from phagolysosomes (Augenstreich et al., 2017; Barczak et al., 2017; Lerner et al., 2017; Quigley et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Camacho et al., 2001

claim: PDIM promotes escape from phagolysosomes.
source: PDIM also promotes pathogenesis in other ways, such as being required for the relative impermeability of the mycobacterial cell wall (Camacho et al., 2001) and in promoting escape from phagolysosomes (Augenstreich et al., 2017; Barczak et al., 2017; Lerner et al., 2017; Quigley et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Augenstreich et al., 2017; Barczak et al., 2017; Lerner et al., 2017; Quigley et al., 2017

claim: Metabolic labeling strategies using unnatural metabolic precursors have been developed to study virulence lipids.
source: To accomplish mechanistic studies of virulence lipids, we and others developed metabolic labeling strategies where unnatural metabolic precursors are fed to growing bacteria (Siegrist et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Siegrist et al., 2015

claim: The unnatural metabolite contains a bioorthogonal functional group that facilitates visualization of macromolecules in living bacteria.
source: The unnatural metabolite contains a bioorthogonal functional group that facilitates visualization of macromolecules in living bacteria (Sletten and Bertozzi, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sletten and Bertozzi, 2009

claim: Trehalose containing lipids can be labeled with azide-functionalized trehalose.
source: An example is the labeling of trehalose containing lipids with azide-functionalized trehalose (Swarts et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Swarts et al., 2012

claim: PDIM spreads into epithelial cells to prevent the recruitment of microbicidal monocytes.
source: We found that the first step in PDIM-mediated pathogenesis is to spread into epithelial cells in order to prevent the recruitment of microbicidal monocytes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: PDIM's methyl-branched fatty acids increased lipid mobility and promoted spread.
source: Structure function analysis revealed that PDIM's methyl-branched fatty acids increased lipid mobility and promoted spread.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: PDIM spreading was dependent on the lipid content of host membranes.
source: Spreading was also dependent on the lipid content of host membranes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Administration of atorvastatin led to a decrease in PDIM spreading.
source: Administration of the cholesterol lowering drug, atorvastatin (Lipitor), led to a decrease in PDIM spreading, and subsequent resistance to mycobacterial infection.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Atorvastatin treatment provided protection from mycobacterial infection.
source: Administration of the cholesterol lowering drug, atorvastatin (Lipitor), led to a decrease in PDIM spreading, and subsequent resistance to mycobacterial infection.
evidence: Supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript

claim: Statin use is associated with a decrease in TB incidence.
source: Our findings provide a mechanistic explanation for the association of statin use with a decrease in TB incidence (Lai et al., 2016) and support their use as a TB preventative therapy.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lai et al., 2016

claim: PDIM lacks unique biosynthetic precursors to facilitate metabolic labeling.
source: PDIM lacks unique biosynthetic precursors to facilitate metabolic labeling (Onwueme et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Onwueme et al., 2005

claim: PDIM is removed following petroleum ether extraction.
source: However, PDIM is removed following petroleum ether extraction (Moliva et al., 2019), a technique used to remove and add back mycomembrane lipids (Silva et al., 1985).
evidence: Supported by citations to Moliva et al., 2019 and Silva et al., 1985

claim: Petroleum ether extraction did not affect the growth of M. marinum in culture.
source: Similar to reports on M. tuberculosis and M. bovis, we validated that petroleum ether extraction did not affect the growth of M. marinum in culture (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and extracted lipids did not repopulate the mycomembrane following the first few days in culture (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; Indrigo et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and citation to Indrigo et al., 2003

claim: Extracted lipids did not repopulate the mycomembrane following the first few days in culture.
source: Similar to reports on M. tuberculosis and M. bovis, we validated that petroleum ether extraction did not affect the growth of M. marinum in culture (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and extracted lipids did not repopulate the mycomembrane following the first few days in culture (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B; Indrigo et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B and citation to Indrigo et al., 2003

claim: Delipidated bacteria were attenuated for growth in zebrafish.
source: Following infection of zebrafish (Figure 1B) delipidated bacteria were attenuated for growth and this phenotype was rescued upon recoating (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D

claim: Recoating delipidated bacteria rescued the growth attenuation phenotype.
source: Following infection of zebrafish (Figure 1B) delipidated bacteria were attenuated for growth and this phenotype was rescued upon recoating (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and D

claim: M. marinum mutants in PDIM synthesis (∆mas) and localization to the mycomembrane (∆mmpL7) trigger TLR/Myd88-dependent immune responses.
source: M. marinum mutants in PDIM synthesis (∆mas) and localization to the mycomembrane (∆mmpL7) trigger TLR/Myd88-dependent immune responses (Cambier et al., 2014b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cambier et al., 2014b

claim: Myd88 signaling leads to the recruitment of activated monocytes that can clear bacteria in an inducible nitric oxide synthase-dependent fashion.
source: Myd88 signaling leads to the recruitment of activated monocytes that can clear bacteria in an inducible nitric oxide synthase-dependent fashion.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge from previous work

claim: PDIM-sufficient wildtype bacteria recruit permissive monocytes downstream of the chemokine CCL2.
source: PDIM-sufficient wildtype bacteria do not elicit this response and instead recruit a comparable number of permissive monocytes downstream of the chemokine CCL2 (Cambier et al., 2014b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cambier et al., 2014b

claim: Wildtype bacteria recoated with ∆mmpL7 lipids were attenuated for growth.
source: Following infection, wildtype control and wildtype bacteria recoated with wildtype lipids grew normally whereas wildtype bacteria recoated with ∆mmpL7 lipids were attenuated for growth (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F

claim: ∆mmpL7 bacteria recoated with wildtype lipids grew at wildtype bacterial rates.
source: Conversely, ∆mmpL7 bacteria were attenuated for growth, as expected, unless they were recoated with wildtype lipids, in which case they grew at wildtype bacterial rates (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F

claim: The dependence on Myd88 to recruit monocytes to ∆mmpL7 bacteria was abolished with wildtype lipids.
source: Using an antisense morpholino to knockdown Myd88 (Bates et al., 2007), we also found that the dependence on Myd88 to recruit monocytes to ∆mmpL7 bacteria was abolished with wildtype lipids (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and citation to Bates et al., 2007

claim: The PDIM present on the surface of the bacterium from the onset of infection is required and sufficient to promote virulence.
source: Furthermore, our data suggest that the PDIM present on the surface of the bacterium from the onset of infection is required and sufficient to promote virulence, as mutants unable to replenish PDIM on their surfaces become infectious when they are recoated with wildtype lipids.
evidence: Supported by inference from experimental data

claim: Either PDIM or PNDIM can promote infection in mice.
source: Either lipid can promote infection in mice (Siméone et al., 2007), suggesting chemical flexibility at this site with regards to virulence.
evidence: Supported by citation to Siméone et al., 2007

claim: Recoating bacteria with lipids containing azido-DIM followed by click reaction with DIBO-488 resulted in a ~100-fold increase in fluorescence.
source: Recoating of delipidated bacteria with lipids containing azido-DIM, followed by a copper-free click reaction with the cyclooctyne fluorophore DIBO-488 (Figure 2B) resulted in a ~100-fold increase in fluorescence (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Fluorescence from azido-DIM labeling was membrane-associated.
source: Confocal microscopy revealed the fluorescence to be membrane-associated (Figure 2D and E), suggesting incorporation into the mycomembrane.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and E

claim: Adding back native DIMs or azido-DIM to DIM-depleted lipids prior to recoating rescued DIM-depleted bacteria's growth attenuation.
source: Importantly, we found that adding back native DIMs or azido-DIM to DIM-depleted lipids prior to recoating and labeling (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) rescued DIM-depleted bacteria's growth attenuation (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F

claim: DIM-488 spread away from bacteria into infected macrophage membranes.
source: DIM-488 spread away from bacteria into infected macrophage membranes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: The spreading of DIM-488 was dynamic in nature, with DIM-488 moving relative to host cells.
source: Real-time imaging revealed that the spreading was dynamic in nature, with DIM-488 moving relative to host cells (Video 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Video 1

claim: As early as 3 hr post-infection (hpi), DIM-488 had spread into infected macrophage membranes.
source: As early as 3 hr post-infection (hpi), DIM-488 had spread into infected macrophage membranes, directly adjacent to infecting bacteria (Figure 3A, arrows) and at more distal membrane sites (Figure 3A, arrow heads).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: Spreading of DIM-488 increased across macrophage membranes by 3 days post-infection (dpi).
source: Spreading increased across macrophage membranes by 3 days post-infection (dpi) (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: Similar spreading was seen when azido-DIM was conjugated to DIBO-647.
source: Similar spreading was seen when azido-DIM was conjugated to DIBO-647 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C), suggesting that the lipid, not the fluorescent probe, was responsible for this phenotype.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and C

claim: PDIM spreading increased as infection progressed.
source: Using this number as a proxy for lipid spread, we saw an increase in spreading as infection progressed (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: PDIM spreading occurred following infection of THP-1 macrophages in culture.
source: Spreading also occurred following infection of THP-1 macrophages in culture (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E

claim: PDIM spreading was not a result of homeostatic lipid turnover.
source: Finally, PDIM spreading was not a result of homeostatic lipid turnover. DIM-488 labeled bacteria were fluorescent following 3 days in culture (Figure 3D), and signal remained localized to the cell wall (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and E

claim: PDIM spreading away from bacteria only occurs following interactions with host cells.
source: Thus, PDIM spreading away from bacteria only occurs following interactions with host cells.
evidence: Supported by inference from experimental data

claim: M. tuberculosis PDIM occupies cultured macrophage membranes.
source: These results were consistent with a recent report that M. tuberculosis PDIM occupies cultured macrophage membranes (Augenstreich et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Augenstreich et al., 2019

claim: Recoating does not appreciably influence the spreading dynamics of mycomembrane lipids.
source: We found equal spreading of the total pool of fluorophore-labeled glycolipids (Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F). Thus, recoating does not appreciably influence the spreading dynamics of mycomembrane lipids.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1F

claim: PDIM has been suggested to interact with the protein substrates of the type VII secretion system ESX-1, including EsxA.
source: PDIM has been suggested to interact with the protein substrates of the type VII secretion system ESX-1, including EsxA (Barczak et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Barczak et al., 2017

claim: PDIM and EsxA are both required for cytosolic escape from phagolysosomes.
source: PDIM and EsxA are both required for cytosolic escape from phagolysosomes (Osman et al., 2020; Quigley et al., 2017; van der Wel et al., 2007), where PDIM is suggested to enhance the pore-forming activity of EsxA through its ability to infiltrate macrophage membranes (Augenstreich et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Osman et al., 2020; Quigley et al., 2017; van der Wel et al., 2007; Augenstreich et al., 2017

claim: There was no difference in DIM-488 spreading kinetics between wildtype and ∆RD1 M. marinum.
source: There was no difference in DIM-488 spreading kinetics between wildtype and ∆RD1 M. marinum (Figure 3G), suggesting that EsxA does not influence PDIM spreading.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G

claim: EsxA does not influence PDIM spreading.
source: There was no difference in DIM-488 spreading kinetics between wildtype and ∆RD1 M. marinum (Figure 3G), suggesting that EsxA does not influence PDIM spreading.
evidence: Supported by inference from experimental data shown in Figure 3G

claim: PDIM has been shown to promote phagocytosis of extracellular bacteria.
source: Besides playing a role in cytosolic escape, PDIM has also been shown to promote phagocytosis of extracellular bacteria (Astarie-Dequeker et al., 2009; Augenstreich et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Astarie-Dequeker et al., 2009 and Augenstreich et al., 2019

claim: There was no measurable difference in the rate of phagocytosis of wildtype or ∆mmpL7 bacteria in zebrafish.
source: There was no measurable difference in the rate of phagocytosis of wildtype or ∆mmpL7 bacteria (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H

claim: Wildtype bacteria needed to reside within resident macrophages in order to recruit permissive monocytes.
source: One clue to the timing of PDIM's role in virulence was the kinetics of the myeloid response. Wildtype bacteria needed to reside within resident macrophages in order to recruit permissive monocytes.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge from previous work

claim: PDIM-deficient bacteria recruited microbicidal monocytes independent of and concurrent to resident macrophages.
source: In contrast, PDIM-deficient bacteria recruited microbicidal monocytes independent of and concurrent to resident macrophages (Cambier et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cambier et al., 2017

claim: DIM-488 from bacteria contacting endothelium had spread away from the bacteria onto the surrounding tissue.
source: We found that the DIM-488 from bacteria contacting endothelium had spread away from the bacteria onto the surrounding tissue (Figure 4B, arrows).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: DIM-488 spreading into labeled epithelial plasma membranes was observed.
source: To confirm PDIM spreading into epithelial membranes, we infected human A549 epithelial cells whose plasma membranes were labeled with Alexa-fluor 594 wheat germ agglutinin. We observed DIM-488 spreading into labeled epithelial plasma membranes (Figure 4C, arrows).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Preceding any appreciable spreading onto macrophages, DIM-488 had already spread onto epithelial cells by 2 hpi.
source: Preceding any appreciable spreading onto macrophages, DIM-488 had already spread onto epithelial cells by 2 hpi (Figure 4D yellow outlines, and Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and 4E

claim: Mycobacteria spread PDIM onto epithelial cells prior to interactions with macrophages.
source: These data suggest that mycobacteria spread PDIM onto epithelial cells prior to interactions with macrophages, and that this spread PDIM remains within these epithelial cells even after bacteria are phagocytosed by macrophages.
evidence: Supported by inference from experimental data

claim: DIM-488 spreading still occurs in the absence of macrophages.
source: By depleting macrophages from zebrafish larva using clodronate-loaded liposomes (Bernut et al., 2014), we confirmed that DIM-488 spreading still occurs in the absence of macrophages (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F and citation to Bernut et al., 2014

claim: PDIM spreads onto epithelial cells independent of and prior to macrophage phagocytosis.
source: These data demonstrate that PDIM spreads onto epithelial cells independent of and prior to macrophage phagocytosis.
evidence: Supported by inference from experimental data

claim: Increased membrane fluidity promotes membrane mixing.
source: It is well established that increased membrane fluidity, a feature influenced by the mobility of individual membrane lipids, promotes membrane mixing (Howell et al., 1972).
evidence: Supported by citation to Howell et al., 1972

claim: The mycomembrane of Mycobacterium smegmatis is relatively immobile.
source: Previous studies from our lab found that the mycomembrane of Mycobacterium smegmatis is relatively immobile by using fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP) of metabolically labeled trehalose monomycolate (TMM) (Rodriguez-Rivera et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rodriguez-Rivera et al., 2017

claim: Around 40% of TMM-488 labeled lipids were mobile in M. marinum.
source: Using the metabolic label 6-azido-trehalose (Swarts et al., 2012) followed by reaction with DIBO-488 to track TMM (TMM-488), we found very little recovery following photobleaching of TMM-488, with only around 40% of the labeled lipids being mobile (Figure 5A–C, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A

claim: DIM-488 recovery was very efficient, with a half-life of 3 s and around 95% of the signal being mobile.
source: When we assessed PDIM, we found DIM-488 recovery to be very efficient, with a half-life of 3 s and around 95% of the signal being mobile (Figure 5A–C, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A–C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: PDIM lipids are more mobile than TMM lipids.
source: Thus, PDIM lipids are more mobile than TMM lipids.
evidence: Supported by inference from experimental data

claim: TMM-488 failed to spread onto epithelial cells at 2 hpi.
source: If increased membrane fluidity and lipid mobility promote membrane mixing, then TMM should not be able to spread into host cells as efficiently as PDIM does. Indeed, we found that TMM-488 failed to spread onto epithelial cells at 2 hpi (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D

claim: TMM spreading was detected only when bacteria are within macrophages at 24 hpi.
source: Only when bacteria are within macrophages at 24 hpi was TMM spreading detected (Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C

claim: Even in the absence of macrophages, TMM-488 spreading was negligible.
source: Even in the absence of macrophages, where bacteria have a prolonged contact time with epithelial cells, TMM-488 spreading was negligible (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E

claim: Lipid mobility correlates with the ability to spread into host epithelial membranes.
source: Thus, lipid mobility correlates with the ability to spread into host epithelial membranes.
evidence: Supported by inference from experimental data

claim: Fixation with 4% PFA + 1% glutaraldehyde resulted in an almost 80% reduction in the mobile fraction of DIM-488.
source: However, fixation with 4% PFA + 1% glutaraldehyde (GA), a more effective fixative for membrane-associated proteins (Huebinger et al., 2018), resulted in an almost 80% reduction in the mobile fraction of DIM-488 (Figure 5F,G and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F, G and Figure 5—figure supplement 2, and citation to Huebinger et al., 2018

claim: PFA+GA treatment decreased DIM-488 spread onto epithelial cells at 2 hpi.
source: PFA+GA treatment decreased DIM-488 spread onto epithelial cells at 2 hpi (Figure 5H and I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H and I

claim: Fixed DIM-488 did not spread into epithelial membranes following a 24 hr infection of macrophage-depleted zebrafish.
source: Likewise, fixed DIM-488 did not spread into epithelial membranes following a 24 hr infection of macrophage-depleted zebrafish (Figure 5J).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5J

claim: Fixed DIM-488 did not spread onto A549 epithelial cells after 24 hr.
source: Nor did it spread onto A549 epithelial cells after 24 hr (Figure 5K).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5K

claim: PDIM's mobility promotes spreading into epithelial membranes.
source: Together these results suggest that PDIM's mobility promotes spreading into epithelial membranes.
evidence: Supported by inference from experimental data

claim: Saturated lipids form closely packed assemblies giving rise to more rigid bilayers.
source: Saturated lipids form closely packed assemblies giving rise to more rigid bilayers, while unsaturated lipids do not pack as tightly and produce more fluid bilayers.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge

claim: Methyl branches on otherwise saturated lipids have been shown to increase membrane fluidity.
source: Methyl branches on otherwise saturated lipids have also been shown to increase membrane fluidity (Budin et al., 2018; Poger et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Budin et al., 2018 and Poger et al., 2014

claim: DIF-488 was not as mobile as DIM-488, with only ~50% in the mobile fraction.
source: FRAP studies confirmed that DIBO-488 labeled azido-DIF (DIF-488) was not as mobile as DIM-488, with only ~50% in the mobile fraction (Figure 6B,C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B, C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C

claim: DIF-488 failed to spread onto epithelial cells at two hpi.
source: Upon zebrafish infection, DIF-488 failed to spread onto epithelial cells at two hpi (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D–F

claim: DIF-488 was capable of spreading into macrophage membranes at later timepoints.
source: However, similar to other mycobacterial lipids (Beatty et al., 2000) including TMM (Figure 5A), DIF-488 was capable of spreading into macrophage membranes at later timepoints (Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D and E, and citation to Beatty et al., 2000

claim: PDIM's mobility, mediated by its methyl-branched lipid tails, promotes its ability to spread into epithelial membranes.
source: Thus, PDIM's mobility, mediated by its methyl-branched lipid tails, promotes its ability to spread into epithelial membranes.
evidence: Supported by inference from experimental data

claim: Wildtype M. marinum must be alive in order to stimulate resident macrophages to express CCL2 to recruit permissive monocytes.
source: Wildtype M. marinum must be alive in order to stimulate resident macrophages to express CCL2 to recruit permissive monocytes (Cambier et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cambier et al., 2017

claim: PDIM-deficient M. marinum do not depend on resident macrophages to recruit bactericidal monocytes and do so in a manner independent of bacterial viability.
source: In contrast, PDIM-deficient M. marinum do not depend on resident macrophages to recruit bactericidal monocytes and do so in a manner independent of bacterial viability (Cambier et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cambier et al., 2017

claim: Heat-killed mycobacteria do not recruit monocytes.
source: We confirmed that heat-killed mycobacteria do not recruit monocytes (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A

claim: PFA-treated bacteria which can spread PDIM did not recruit monocytes.
source: Likewise, PFA-treated bacteria which can also spread PDIM did not recruit monocytes (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A

claim: PFA+GA treated bacteria recruited monocytes to a similar extent as live bacteria.
source: However, monocyte recruitment toward PFA+GA treated bacteria, which do not spread PDIM, phenocopied heat-killed ∆mmpL7 M. marinum; even though they are not viable, they recruited monocytes to a similar extent as live bacteria (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A

claim: Monocyte recruitment toward PFA+GA treated bacteria was downstream of Myd88 signaling.
source: Moreover, this monocyte recruitment was now downstream of Myd88 signaling (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B

claim: PDIM spreading into epithelial membranes is required to prevent Myd88-dependent recruitment of monocytes.
source: Taken together these data demonstrate that PDIM spreading into epithelial membranes is required to prevent Myd88-dependent recruitment of monocytes.
evidence: Supported by inference from experimental data

claim: PDIM-deficient bacteria are killed by Myd88-recruited monocytes.
source: Not only are PDIM-deficient bacteria killed by Myd88-recruited monocytes but co-infected PDIM-expressing bacteria are as well (Cambier et al., 2014b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Cambier et al., 2014b

claim: Co-infection with PFA+GA treated bacteria caused attenuation of wildtype bacteria.
source: Only co-infection with PFA+GA treated bacteria caused attenuation of wildtype bacteria (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C

claim: Attenuation of wildtype bacteria by co-infection with PFA+GA treated bacteria was dependent on Myd88.
source: Moreover, this attenuation was dependent on Myd88 (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D

claim: Recoating with PDIF does not rescue bacterial growth.
source: Consistent with the requirement for PDIM to spread into epithelial cells to promote virulence, we found that recoating with PDIF does not rescue bacterial growth (Figure 7E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E

claim: Cholesterol has been reported to modulate macrophage interactions with mycobacteria.
source: Cholesterol has been reported to modulate macrophage interactions with mycobacteria (Gatfield and Pieters, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gatfield and Pieters, 2000

claim: 36% of the lipid extracted from Mycobacterium bovis harvested from necrotic mouse lung was found to be host cholesterol.
source: However, three lines of evidence suggest a macrophage-independent relationship between mycobacteria and cholesterol: (1) 36% of the lipid extracted from Mycobacterium bovis harvested from necrotic mouse lung (where macrophages are sparse) was found to be host cholesterol Kondo and Kanai, 1976;
evidence: Supported by citation to Kondo and Kanai, 1976

claim: Mycobacterial-associated cholesterol was isolated as a mixture with PDIM.
source: (2) mycobacterial-associated cholesterol was isolated as a mixture with PDIM Kondo and Kanai, 1976;
evidence: Supported by citation to Kondo and Kanai, 1976

claim: M. tuberculosis grown in culture can sequester cholesterol to its outer mycomembrane, a process dependent on mycomembrane lipids.
source: (3) M. tuberculosis grown in culture can sequester cholesterol to its outer mycomembrane, a process dependent on mycomembrane lipids (Brzostek et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brzostek et al., 2009

claim: Only wildtype M. marinum could sequester cholesterol to their mycomembrane.
source: We found that only wildtype M. marinum could sequester cholesterol to their mycomembrane (Figure 8A and B).

claim: Both wildtype and ∆mmpL7 M. marinum could equally sequester azido-PE.
